The concept is solid and grounded in a real, well-articulated problem, but it is more credible on need than on differentiation and defensibility.

Strengths: The pain point is concrete and verifiable. Small cities lack reliable vacancy data, rely on stale assessor lists, windshield surveys, or tribal knowledge, and increasingly need data-backed evidence to win grants and prove outcomes afterward. The 'baseline for grant applications' angle ties the product to money flows, which gives it a clear ROI story. The solution logic (cross-referencing utility inactivity with mail-delivery vacancy flags) is intuitive and plausible, and the non-technical map/export output fits the user profile. The founders have relevant proximity to the problem (planning office experience, modeling, engineering), have built a working prototype, and received positive qualitative feedback from two city offices and a regional group. The small-city focus is a sensible wedge, since larger vendors are priced and designed for bigger buyers.

Weaknesses: Uniqueness is weak. The plan itself concedes the signal-fusion approach is not unique in principle, the space is crowded, and incumbents could add similar features quickly. The claimed advantage is positioning (simplicity, price, focus), which is easily imitated and not a durable moat. The core value proposition also hinges on data access that is unresolved: utility data requires agreements with providers, privacy treatment is unvetted, and mail-delivery data availability is vague. If the data cannot be obtained at scale and cost, the product does not exist. Accuracy is unproven: there is no validation of the scoring against ground truth (precision/recall against field surveys), which is the central question for any estimate-based product. Evidence of demand is thin. Verbal interest is not willingness to pay, there are no signed pilots, and the need is stated rather than quantified (how much staff time or grant dollars are at stake). Municipal buyers have slow procurement, tight budgets, and low price points, so a 'useful' reaction does not equate to a purchasable pain. Alternatives like free assessor data, USPS-derived HUD vacancy data, and university partnerships may be 'good enough' for many cities.

Overall: A genuine, relevant problem with a sensible and well-scoped solution, and a promising early-stage concept, but it reads as a useful feature or data product rather than a clearly unique, compelling offering. Its quality will be determined by three unproven items: secured data access, demonstrated scoring accuracy, and validated willingness to pay. Moderate-to-good concept quality with high execution and data-dependency risk.

Business plan text:

Vacancy Atlas
Vacancy Atlas: Executive Summary
Problem
Small cities face a difficult problem when they try to revitalize their downtowns and
neighborhoods. They often do not know how many storefronts and homes are actually vacant, or
where the vacancies are concentrated. Without that information, it is hard to decide where to
spend limited revitalization funds. A planner in a small city may rely on a windshield survey
done by an intern, a list from the assessor that is a year or two old, or the personal
knowledge of a long-serving staff member. These approaches are slow, expensive in staff time,
and inconsistent from one year to the next.
The stakes are real. Federal and state programs, as well as private foundations, offer funding
for revitalization, but most of them ask applicants to show need with data. Cities that cannot
document their vacancy levels are at a disadvantage when applying. Cities that do receive funds
often cannot show afterward whether the money made a difference, because they never had a
baseline.
Solution
Vacancy Atlas is a data product that estimates vacant storefronts and homes by crossreferencing two kinds of signals: utility activity and mail-delivery status. When a property
has had no active utility account or very low usage for an extended period, and mail-delivery
records flag it as undeliverable or vacant, the likelihood that it is empty is high. Neither
signal is perfect alone, but together they give a more reliable picture than either one. Our
software combines them, assigns each property a vacancy likelihood score, and displays the
results on an easy-to-read map with block-level summaries.
The output is designed for non-technical users. A planner can open the map, filter by
neighborhood or property type, and export a list for grant applications or field verification.
We also provide a short quarterly update so that cities can track change over time.
Market
Our target customers are municipal planning and economic development offices in small and midsized cities, which we define as roughly 20,000 to 150,000 residents. In the United States
there are several hundred such cities in the regions where we plan to start. We also see
regional planning councils, downtown development authorities, and community development
nonprofits as possible buyers. Many of these organizations manage grant programs and need data
to decide where to send funds.
We estimate that if we reach a modest share of these organizations at an annual price in the
low thousands of dollars each, the market is large enough to support a small company. We
recognize that this estimate is rough and that municipal budgets are tight. We plan to refine
it through conversations with pilot customers.
Business Model
We plan to sell annual subscriptions. The base subscription would include access to the vacancy
map, a yearly data refresh, and exports. A higher tier would add quarterly updates and help
with grant applications. We expect pricing to depend on the size of the city. Early pilots may
be offered at a discount or free in exchange for feedback and permission to describe results.
Our costs are mainly data acquisition, cloud hosting, and the time of the founders. The biggest
uncertainty is access to the underlying data. We are exploring agreements with utility
providers and using publicly available delivery-status information, and we are working through
what privacy rules require. We believe that aggregating to the property level without personal
information keeps us on safe ground, but we plan to get legal advice before expanding.

Competition
The space is crowded. Large data companies sell property and demographic data to cities, and
some include vacancy indicators. Several software firms offer planning and permitting platforms
that touch on vacancy. Some cities build their own tools using in-house analysts or university
partners, and many simply use spreadsheets and field surveys. Our advantage is that we focus
only on vacancy and design for small cities that cannot afford large platforms or dedicated
data staff. Our use of utility and mail signals is not unique in principle, but we believe our
focus on simplicity, price, and small-city needs gives us a place in the market. We know that
larger competitors could add similar features, and we will need to move quickly to build
relationships.
Team
Marcus Delgado leads product and customer relations. He is studying urban planning at our
university and has worked part time in a city planning office, where he saw the vacancy problem
firsthand. Priya Raman is responsible for data and modeling. She studies statistics and built
the first version of our scoring approach. Tobias Lindqvist handles software development and
the map interface; he is a computer science student with experience building web applications.
Together we cover planning knowledge, data analysis, and engineering. We do not yet have a team
member with sales experience, and we plan to look for advisors who do.
Milestones and Financials
So far we have defined the core concept, built a working prototype, and registered Vacancy
Atlas LLC. The prototype has been shown to a small number of outside users, including staff at
two city offices and a regional planning group, who gave us feedback on the map and the
scoring. They said the idea was useful, though we do not yet have paying customers or signed
pilot agreements. We also have a website that explains the product.
Our financial position is early. We have spent only small amounts of our own money on hosting
and legal filing. We have not yet generated revenue. Our rough plan is to sign three to five
pilot cities in the next year, convert some of them to paid subscriptions, and reach modest
revenue that covers data and hosting costs by the end of the second year. These projections are
based on assumptions that we have not fully tested, especially the price municipalities are
willing to pay and how quickly they make purchasing decisions.
What We Are Asking For
We are applying to the competition for three things. First, funding to cover data costs,
hosting, and legal advice on data privacy. Second, mentorship from people with experience
selling to local governments, since this is the area where our team is weakest. Third,
introductions to potential pilot cities and data partners. A prize would let us run our first
formal pilots and test whether cities will pay for the product. We are open to feedback on our
model and willing to adjust our approach based on what we learn.
Question: Discuss the overall quality of the business concept or idea. Address whether the offering addresses a real and clearly identified pain or need in a unique and compelling way.
